# Theory: (SUBTITLE HERE)

\chaptermark{Theory}

This chapter summarizes the theoretical contribution of the book. In brief, the primary argument is this: that extensive electoral manipulation requires incumbents to solve considerable principal-agent problems, and that taking this proposition seriously requires us to reframe how we understand the relationship between electoral manipulation and post-election protest. Individuals tasked with illegal election manipulation undertake personal risk to do so, even in authoritarian regimes. Therefore, in order to recruit election-manipulating agents on the front line, incumbents must have command over considerable patronage resources (to reward agents) and be able to credibly assure law-breaking individuals will not face punishment. 

Incumbents who successfully deploy extensive electoral manipulation, therefore have capacities that can be used directly to defeat protest movements that may arise after the election. Patronage resources can be used to demobilize opponents and mobilize clients, and to co-opt social groups, parties, or factions into siding with the regime. Politicized police, security forces, and courts can enable the repression of protesters via the judicial system. The legal impunity for regime agents that can flow from such control over the courts can also be used to intensify the cost of protest, for exam through extra-judicial detentions and violence.

These are direct 'benefits' to incumbents of the capacities needed for extensive election manipulation. *Utilizing* those capacities by rigging the election also sends signals to elites that enhance the regime's durability during protest. Authoritarian leaders face protest risks, but also the risk of elite defection and coups. Indeed, one of the things that makes protest risky for incumbents is the possibility that significant, visible popular discontent will prompt an attempted coup. By rigging the election, the incumbent demonstrates to elites that it has the capacity to solve multi-layered principal-agent problems---signaling its deep pockets, control over the judicial apparatus, and ability to mobilize agents whose incentives do not align with those of the boss. All this makes the incumbent look more durable, which helps keep elites loyal during the protest. The lack of elite support for the protesters---and the provision of support to the incumbent---helps reduce the duration and severity of the post-election protest movement. 

Bluntly put, if incumbents can successfully produce extensive electoral manipulation, they are simultaneously inoculating themselves against the cost of post-election protest. This perspective upends a common expectation in scholarly research and democracy promotion in practice. It is often held that, as electoral manipulation increases in severity, the risk to incumbents also rises in the form of protest risk. This chapter articulates why the opposite can be true: more manipulation can actually make incumbents safer. The remainder of the book then demonstrates empirical evidence in favor of this theory.

This theory models behavior by incumbents, front-line agents, and (potential) regime opponents. In the next three sections, each of these actors' incentives and behaviors are described. The fourth section ties all three together, providing a synthesis and expected outcomes.

## Part 0: Defining manipulation

Over time, scholars have advanced four approaches toward the definition of electoral manipulation. Two of these are rooted in local understandings of election integrity, and two appeal to broader standards [@birch2011]. The first, and simplest, definition of electoral manipulation focuses on whether particular actions are violations of local electoral law. This, of course, poses two difficulties: what is legal in one context may be illegal in another, and---even more problematic---laws themselves may be structured to advantage one party over others. A second approach focuses on local norms, rather than (or in addition to) local legal conditions. Electoral behaviors that may be considered unacceptable in some contexts, may be broadly acceptable in others. This possibility has been especially important in studies of vote-buying, where some scholars have emphasized the coerciveness of the practice (e.g. with monitoring and punishment for defection), while others have emphasized cultures of reciprocity and mutual support which can underpin the vote-buying relationship and lead recipients to view such 'gifts' as legitimate [@Lawson2014;@Nichter2018a;@greeneMoneyCantBuy2024]. 

These local approaches to election integrity have, however, largely given way to approaches that make claims at universality. The third school grounds its understanding of electoral manipulation in international law---in particular the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the UN International Covenant for Civil and Political Rights [@Norris2013]---and the subsequent development of global norms for election management and election monitoring [@kelley2008;@hyde_catch_2011]. Lastly, a fourth approach is grounded in democratic theory; it begins by identifying the elements that are necessary for a democratic election to take place, and defines election manipulation as institutions and behaviors which obstruct those elements. 

Though this last school of thought is founded upon democratic theory espoused by Dahl [-@dahlPolyarchyParticipationOpposition1971], among others, it has perhaps been most clearly articulated in Andreas Schedler's [-@schedler2002] "menu of manipulation." In it, Schedler identifies seven requirements for a democratic election to succeed, ranging from the delegation of power to elected positions (i.e. elected officials must hold real power, rather than ceremonial or ineffective positions) to the irreversibility of electoral outcomes. Other essential features of a democratic election include freedom to form parties and compete in elections, voting eligibility for all full members of the community, free formation and expression of preferences, and fair aggregation of preferences under the principle of 'one person, one vote.'

Here, I follow this latter school of thought for a broad definition of electoral manipulation. To paraphrase Shchedler [-@Schedler2013, p. 83], electoral manipulation in general refers to any and all techniques that limit the choices of political authorities among a community of free and equal citizens. The focus of this book, however, is on a subset of violations of the 'chain of democratic choice;' those tactics which are procedurally illegitimate and *carried out by individuals*. I refer to this class of manipulative tactics as *illicit, individual manipulation.* Election manipulation techniques are procedurally illegitimate when they break the established rules for allocating power [@beethamLegitimationPower2013]. <!--  or more broadly when they depart from the principles of neutrality, fairness, and voice [@vandenbosWhenWeNeed1998;@tylerWhyPeopleObey2006]. [NOTE: More on this from prior work?] -->

Illicit, individual manipulation excludes most examples of formal electoral manipulation identified by Schedler [-@schedler2002], such as the creation of biased electoral rules or longstanding disenfranchisement of groups of citizens. So long as these tactics are procedurally legitimate---insofar as they are adopted according to the law---they do not expose their perpetrators to personal legal risk. Legislators who approve gerrymandered maps, for instance, may expose themselves to some political risks if the decision proves unpopular. But they are unlikely to be charged with a crime for doing so. 


On the other hand, a wide variety of procedurally illegitimate forms of electoral manipulation are enacted by individuals around election time. These include---at minimum---vote-buying, voter pressure, ballot-stuffing, multiple voting, and falsification. This framing includes economic electoral intimidation [@fryeWorkplacePoliticsHow2025] and non-state forms of electoral violence, but would likely exclude officially state-sanctioned electoral violence like police disruption of opposition gatherings [@birchElectoralViolenceCorruption2020]. 

Do illicit, individual forms of manipulation merit book-length investigation? It is a well-developed position in the literature that incumbents should prefer to rely on exactly the opposite kind of manipulation (i.e. formal techniques), which tend to be less visible and thus less damaging to incumbents' legitimacy, and can also be highly reliable [@birch2011;@Norris2013;@Szakonyi2021]. Nevertheless, there are several reasons for scholars to focus on illicit forms of manipulation. 

First, it is this kind of manipulation---falsification, ballot-stuffing, vote-buying, and the like---which forms the backstop to other, more predictable forms of institutional manipulation. Gerrymandered districts and biased electoral systems can backfire when incumbent popularity is low. Even when the genuine opposition has been excluded from the ballot, and there is thus no risk of incumbent defeat, incumbents still often turn to deliberate, personal forms of electoral manipulation; uncompetitive elections tend to depress turnout, which incumbents must compensate for in order to maintain an image of electoral strength.

Moreover, these techniques are theoretically important as the kind that is most likely to spark protest (due to procedural injustice and revealed information about incumbent), *and* as the most likely to be called out by observers. Because procedurally illegitimate forms of manipulation break the rules, they simultaneously increase protest risk (i.e. incur legitimacy costs) and produce individual risk for the perpetrator. The importance of this latter factor, however, has not previously been developed.

## Part 1: What do authoritarian principals want from elections?

Authoritarian leaders face two general threats to their position: mass revolt from below, and removal in an elite coup [@svolik_politics_2012]. These threats create a dilemma: allocating too much of society's resources to elites risks popular revolt, while devoting too much to the collective good can risk a coup by elites in search of a better deal. Incumbents utilize elections and electoral manipulation to help manage this dilemma. Holding elections allows incumbents to gather information about the population and the opposition [@Geddes1989;@Miller2015a;@magaloni2006], as well as on the popularity and effectiveness of subordinates [@blaydes2011]. Elections help incumbents recruit ambitious politicians into their party and manage intra-elite disputes over resource distribution [@lust_okar2006]. Finally, an election which delivers a large margin of victory for the incumbent can send a signal that induces cooperation from other political actors [@magaloni2006].

Of course, holding an election introduces the possibility of losing an election. The first generation of research on electoral manipulation tended to assume that the main function of manipulation was to avoid electoral defeat. The competitiveness of the election and stakes of losing power are the main drivers of manipulation in this tradition. Incumbents have more to gain from election rigging when they are likely to narrowly lose the election without it [@nybladeWhoCheatsWho2008;@lehoucq2002;@kamSecretBallotMarket2017;@Birch2007;@Fukumoto2011], and when the prospect of losing carries significant costs [@ziblatt2009;@baturoDemocracyDictatorshipTerm2014;@acemoglu2005economic;@Schedler2013;@horzElectoralManipulationPolarized2021].  

Subsequent research identified broader benefits of rigged elections for leaders. In Simpser's [-@simpser2013] influential formulation, election manipulation is about more than merely winning elections; when manipulation is excessive and/or blatant, it can communicate information about the regime's resources and capacities. These signals may convince other actors in society that the incumbent is likely to remain in office in the future [@simpser2013].  By setting expectations around regime durability, manipulation can lead other actors in society to cooperate with the incumbent [@gehlbach2015electoral]. Costlier types of election manipulation may send more convincing signals of strength, reducing the likelihood of protest [@Harvey2020].

So, from the incumbent's perspective, electoral manipulation helps achieve electoral victory and can convey information about the incumbent's strength to others. But it also comes with costs. First, there are unavoidable material and organizational costs. Even relatively cost-effective tactics like co-opting employers to pressure voters requires monitoring efforts and rewards for compliant businesses [@frye2014, p. 207]. Agents and brokers engaged in falsification or other types of manipulation must still be organized and compensated [@Langston2009mexico]. Vote-buying, however, is especially costly [@lehoucq2002;@wang2007], and such efforts become increasingly expensive as competitiveness increases [@corstange2018clientelism]. Using detailed data on ruling party expenditures on vote-buying in Taiwan in 1993, Wang and Kurzman [-@wang2007] estimate that a vote-buying effort in a single county could cost more than four million USD (in 1993 dollars)---about twelve times the legal campaign expenditure limit. There are a variety of resources which can be used to manipulate elections---goods, cash, jobs, regulatory pressure or favors, and so on---but all of these are finite and involve trade-offs. Resources deployed to manipulate an election in one area cannot be deployed elsewhere or for another purpose (including lining the incumbent's own pockets). 

Beyond the organizational cost, scholars have also focused on the 'legitimacy cost' of election manipulation [@birch2011]. Legitimacy is understood as an individual's subjective sense that authorities have the right to rule, even if the individual may object to  particular decisions [@Lipset1960]. Greater legitimacy, in turn, makes it more likely that individuals will comply with authorities' demands [@Levi_Sacks2009]. 

The legitimacy cost of electoral manipulation, then, is both psychological and potentially behavioral. A reduction in individuals’ subjective evaluation that elected authorities have the right to govern can be associated with reduced willingness to obey the government [@Schedler2013]. Birch [-@birch2011] cites protest risk explicitly as a cost of manipulation, saying legitimacy costs "...can be understood in terms of the proportion of the population that can be expected to acquiesce to having their contribution to public choice taken from them or distorted." As a result, she writes, "The capacity for popular mobilization and protest ought to be negatively correlated with electoral malpractice" (p. 58). Schedler [-@Schedler2013] has further usefully defined legitimacy costs as a function of the severity and visiblity of the manipulation employed (p. 274).

This understanding of the cost of electoral manipulation---as a reduction in legitimacy and associated increase in the risk of mass protest---has been widespread in the literature. It has been especially foundational to formal models of electoral manipulation, where loss of support and/or protest risk often stand as the main downside for incumbents [@Little2015;@littleFraudMonitoringNoncompetitive2015;@chernykh2015third]. For instance, Magaloni [-@magaloni2010] writes that, "The legitimacy loss of fraud can be conceived as the costs to the autocrat of damaging its reputation before its own supporters and/or before the international community." 

Protest risk as the cost of manipulation also figures in less formal theory. It is central to the literature on election monitoring [@hyde_2012_marinov;@kelley2012] Manipulated elections can serve as a focal point for citizens' diverse grievances, raising the likelihood of protest [@tucker2007;@higashijimaDictatorsDilemmaBallot2022]. And, by the same token, election fraud figures prominently in general theories of electoral protest.  Higashijima [-@higashijimaDictatorsDilemmaBallot2022] writes that elections can destabIlize authoritarian rule when "a dictator engages in excessive electoral manipulation to such a degree that it... makes it difficult for opposition leaders to correctly estimate the dictator’s true strength and makes it easy to capitalize on popular grievance, provoking popular protest" (p. 10). His analysis shows that excessive electoral fraud makes popular protest initiation more likely [@higashijimaDictatorsDilemmaBallot2022].

In sum, when holding an election, the existing literature expects incumbents to try to optimize across several goals: to win the election, to send signals of 'strength' to other political actors, to manage organizational costs, and to minimize legitimacy costs. As we will see in [PART 4], integrating principal-agent problems more fully in the theory of manipulation shows that the most fundamental 'legitimacy cost'---the risk of losing office in a revolt---is actually declines as electoral manipulation increases. To show why this is, we next turn to a discussion of low-level agents' incentives to participate in manipulation efforts.

## Part 2: What do front-line agents want?

Incumbents who wish to manipulate elections extensively cannot do so alone; they require cooperation from a large network of subordinates to bribe or pressure voters, stuff ballot boxes, or forge results. These individuals can be more or less closely linked to the incumbent's party. They can be partisan activists [@stokesBrokersVotersClientelism2013] or election officials [@baderRolePrecinctCommissions2017;@Sjoberg2016], independent neighborhood brokers [@langstonWhyClientelistBrokers2023], local mayors and civil servants [@maresCoreVotersCurse2018], public sector employees [@Forrat2018], managers of workplaces [@fryeWorkplacePoliticsHow2025;@cohnpostarVoteYourBread2021], and so on.    

These individuals must be willing to expend resources and undertake personal risks far from the center of power. The earliest generation of modern research on electoral manipulation often assumed, for the sake of parsimony, that whatever level of manipulation the incumbent ordered was smoothly carried out. A subsequent generation of research on authoritarian politics has emphasized the risks incumbents face from their subordinates [@svolik_politics_2012;@svolikPowerSharingLeadership2009;@magaloni2008credible], the abundance of principal-agent problems in such environments [@rundlett2016deliver;@Harvey2019;@tysonAgencyProblemUnderlying2018], and the difficulty of monitoring low-level agents [@Larreguy2016;@Boix2013]. It is, consequently, no small feat to mobilize thousands or tens of thousands of individuals to stuff ballot boxes, bribe voters, or falsify election returns.

Doing so requires that the incumbent have considerable influence over high-level actors like political party leaders, regional governors, big business owners, and so on. These high-level actors, in turn, must be able to exercise influence over meso-level actors like regional legislators, mayors, town councilors, and firm directors, etc. Finally, these meso-level actors must be able to exercise influence over the front-line agents---precinct election officials, floor managers, low-level civil servants, party operatives, etc.---and even individual voters themselves. As these examples suggest, election manipulation networks are usually pyramidal, with actors at each level responsible for overseeing a larger number of actors at the next level down [@hale_patronal_2014]. Political candidates’ dependence on agents raises the possibility that agents’ may not always behave as the boss might prefer [@rundlett2016deliver] These are not easy problems for incumbents to solve, as actors at every step in the chain may have incentives to misrepresent their loyalty and effort on the boss's behalf [@harveyWhyAllowLocal2022].

While both principals and agents may participate in electoral manipulation, their underlying incentives diverge in important ways. Political principals benefit directly from manipulation [@greene_why_2007;@magaloni2006] since it improves their chances of winning close elections [@lehoucq2002] and widens their margin of victory [@gehlbach2015electoral;@simpser2013]. They gain utility, in other words, from each added vote. Agents, by contrast, are primarily motivated by credible access to patronage resources: the jobs, rents, and other benefits that come with participation in a political leader's network [@diaz2006federalism;@lust_okar2006;@reuter2012subnational]. A neighborhood broker, for instance, may seek a local administrative position through which rents can be extracted [@zarazaga2014brokers], while a schoolteacher serving as an election administrator in Russia may participate in ballot-stuffing only to preserve her own salary or benefits [@Forrat2018]. For example, Russia’s primary election-monitoring group recorded numerous incidents of voters being pressured to support the ruling party by their employers during the 2011 election. The following example is representative:

> At Kindergarten No. 620 [in St. Petersburg], a meeting was held in which employees were compelled to take absentee ballots in order to vote on school grounds. It was said that otherwise the district would be cut off from funding, but that voting by absentee would be rewarded with cash bonuses and time off. ...It was pointed out that [Duma] Deputy S. Shatunovskii (a member of United Russia) had done a lot for the district and it was necessary to support him [@golos_analytical_2011].


As the anecdote illustrates, local school administrators pressured their employees with the risk of job loss and the promise of bonuses, in order to remain within the ruling party’s patronage network. This sort of voter pressure / vote-buying is common in sectors that rely on state patronage for their success [@frye2014]. Other forms of manipulation which rely more directly on state actors, such as ballot-stuffing or falsification of results, are also carried out in order to retain access to patronage. Principals in electoral authoritarian regimes tie access to the state and its associated opportunities for rents and patronage to electoral success [@diaz2006federalism;@lust_okar2006;@reuter2012subnational;@reuter2015], and can use the same resources to penalize opponents [@mcmann2006economic]. This creates a powerful incentive for local agents to boost the principal’s vote-share by whatever means are available, including misuse of the election administration apparatus, in order to remain within the privileged network. 

Agents are recruited into election manipulation efforts by promises of patronage. However, since electoral manipulation of this kind is illegal (even in the most authoritarian cases), agents also want to be assured they will avoid punishment for breaking the law.  An individual caught illegally tampering with the election can face criminal, civil, professional, reputational, and personal risks. They may face civil lawsuits or criminal prosecution, which---even in the most favorable circumstances---requires them to retain legal representation and devote time to the case. Loss in court can result in fines, prison time, or loss of official position. In some contexts, conviction of a crime can lead to professional penalties, including dismissal. Even probation, a relatively lenient penalty, brings restrictions on an individual's movements and activities, and increased monitoring by the state. These are all possible negative consequences for participating in election manipulation, which weigh against the inducements offered by the principal. Crucially, as I argue below, these risks exist even if the incumbent remains in power.

### Legal risk in authoritarian regimes

Even the most closed authoritarian regimes have competing incentives here. On the one hand, they may desire to protect their agents in order to promote manipulation in the future. On the other hand, they have incentives to allow a degree of judicial independence and transparency. More independent courts enhance regime legitimacy, reduce corruption, and increase investment [@Moustafa2008;@tsaiWhatMakesAnticorruption2022]. Furthermore, by allowing some agents to be exposed and punished, the incumbent may burnish the overall image of the election. 'Of course, a small number of our supporters were overzealous and bent the law,' this approach implies, 'but the legal system will handle these exceptional cases.' Naturally this is a bad place to be for the scapegoated agent.


Consequently, courts in non-democratic regimes do sometimes act to redress low-level electoral violations. For example, Popova [-@popova2012politicized] finds that district courts in Russia were more likely to hear election-related cases in competitive districts, and that pro-government candidates were not systematically more likely to win than pro-opposition candidates (pp. 94-95). More dramatically, beginning in the 1970s, the combination of legal reforms criminalizing certain electoral malpractices, the creation of more independent bodies to enforce those laws, and public and legal contestation by opposition parties largely cleaned up elections in authoritarian Mexico [@serraVoteBuyingIllegal2016;@eisenstadt_courting_2003]. Ultimately these changes helped usher out the ruling PRI after seven decades in power. 

Courts often hear charges against election officials for election tampering, but they can also adjudicate cases against ordinary individuals accused of other types of manipulation:  vote-buying, voter pressure, voter impersonation, and multiple voting [@Orozco-Henriquez2010]. Since authoritarian rulers have incentives to create a court system that does, on occasion, rule against the regime's supporters [@ginsburg_rule_2008;@popova2012politicized;@hendleyEverydayLawRussia2017;@Harvey2022], this can create acute risks for front-line agents in cases where exposure is more likely. In 1999, for example, Russian courts ruled against election commissioners accused of electoral malfeasance (including fraud allegations) in about half of cases [@Solomon2004]. A report on the punishment of election commissioners for violations of the election law from 2009 to 2015 in Russia found that, while most infractions are punished by small fines, significant punishments could be brought in cases with sufficient local political pressure [@golos__2015]. In some cases recorded by the monitoring group, election commissioners were found guilty of criminal offenses and faced stiff penalties, including fines of over half an average annual salary. Chapter 6, in this volume, shows further evidence of such risks in modern, more authoritarian Russia.

Such risks may have high or low probabilities of being realized, depending on individual context. Local agents are valuable to principals in part because of their deep knowledge of their local environment, which better enables them to monitor voters, distribute clientelistic benefits, or otherwise alter election results [@frye2014;@zarazaga2014brokers]. However, this local knowledge also allows agents to make strategic judgments about the level of local risk involved in manipulating an election in particular ways. They may abstain, or---in more competitive settings---may stop mobilizing voters or switch parties if the status quo becomes too risky [@stokes2013brokers, pp. 121-126]. 

The risk to agents can be thought of as a multiplicative index of of two factors: the probability that a particular electoral misdeed will be exposed, and the probability that it can be attributed to a specific individual. Holding one factor constant, increasing or decreasing the other raises or lowers the overall risk accordingly. For example, consider the following ideal-type scenarios. In the first, the risk of exposure is high but the risk of individual attribution is low; in the second, the positions are reversed. 

In one case, an agent is tasked with entering a polling place under a false name and stuffing several ballots in the box. Election monitors will monitor the count, but not the full day's vote. The probability that this electoral misdeed can be detected after the fact is very high: the number of ballots received will not match the number of ballots issued. However, the probability that the crime will be specifically attributed to our agent is very low; unless caught in the act by observers, it is difficult to know when the illicit ballots entered the ballot box or at whose hand. As such, the risk to the agent in this case is minimal.

Now consider a second agent, the chairperson of an election commission tasked with falsifying the results in her precinct. There are no election monitors, and the other members of the commission represent parties co-opted by the incumbent. The probability of attribution is very high---only the chairperson can record and transmit the results, and her actions are likely witnessed by other commissioners. However, the lack of independent or opposition-party observation reduces the probability of exposure to nearly zero. This agent, too, has little to fear. 

When the probabilities of exposure and attribution are both positive and sizable, however, the calculus begins to change. For instance, if we change the latter scenario such that the precinct is well-monitored, or there are active opposition-party members on the commission, it becomes much more likely that the chairperson's falsification will be exposed. In that case, she may face real risks of facing personal accountability for breaking the electoral law.

While prior studies have not investigated agent risk in depth, there is empirical evidence on the correlation between *exposure* risk and manipulation. For example, the presence of election monitors makes it more likely that manipulation will be exposed [@kelley2012], and can deter manipulation [@hyde_catch_2011;@sjoberg_autocratic_2013] at particular polling sites. Similarly, when opposition parties have limited or no representation on election commissions, pro-incumbent manipulation is harder to expose and easier to accomplish [@kovalov_electoral_2014;@bader_osce_2012;@calingaert_election_2006]. <!--Monitors are more likely to be present in politically open territories [@Buzin2016], and more likely to be effective in more competitive districts [@asunka2017electoral].--> Local media can also play an important role in exposing criminal corruption [@usherHowLoudDoes2024], of which election manipulation can be an example.

In cases where a dominant party machine exercises control over regional courts, opposition party figures are less likely to pursue complaints in regional courts [@popova2006], reducing the risk to agents of engaging in manipulation.  Opposition parties know that criminal-legal risk is part of agents' calculations. In the 2003 State Duma election, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation lost 61 seats, more than half of its delegation. In an essay in the party newspaper *Pravda Rossii*, party leader Gennady Zyuganov highlighted the importance of holding election manipulators to account in the courts:

> "Hundreds, thousands of cases of vote-rigging, forgery and manipulation have been identified. Not a single fact of fraud must be overlooked. We must go to the courts and seek the prosecution of the fraudsters. This is a special and very important front of the struggle.... If we can identify and punish the falsifiers, we will strengthen popular democracy and it will be easier for us to win in the future" [@zyuganov2003].

The same edition of the paper also depicted the unfairness of the election outcome in an editorial cartoon, shown in Figure \@ref(fig:cartoon). In it, ballots in United Russia's favor are made to weigh more by a television and a policeman's baton---two pillars of the incumbent's 'administrative resources' used to bias elections. 

```{r cartoon, out.width="80%", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Post-election cartoon showing United Russia's advantages: control over the media and police"}
knitr::include_graphics("pravda_rossii_cartoon.png")
```


To summarize, low-level actors tasked with rigging elections are motivated by patronage offers weighed against the risk of punishment (which can be further decomposed into the risk that an electoral crime will be exposed and the risk that it will be attributed to the agent). These agents will be more willing to engage in electoral manipulation when the rewards are high and the risks are low. The rewards are well-understood; they typically involve participation in the incumbent's patronage network (providing access to jobs, career advancement, opportunities for enrichment, favors, and so on). The risks have been less well understood. 

Even in authoritarian regimes, incumbents have an incentive to permit the independent operation of the justice system to some degree. Even where he has firm control over the police and the courts, the incumbent may still have incentives to allow a small proportion of agents to be penalized for electoral crimes, in order to bolster the overall legitimacy of the election and the regime. While prospective agents cannot know *a priori* whether they will be protected, they can use their local knowledge to estimate the risk of exposure and subsequent punishment. Where the possibility of exposure and attribution is perceived to be high (relative to the patronage rewards), agents should be less willing to take risks to manipulate on the incumbent's behalf. However, as shown in [RUSSIA CHAPTER], this dynamic does not mean that elections will necessarily be cleaner; instead, risk pushes agents into harder-to-detect forms of manipulation that are costlier to incumbents.

### Case studies: Patronage, agent risk, and election integrity in early modern democracy

\sectionmark{Illicit manipulation in early democracies}

Naturally, the earliest entrepreneurs of election manipulation are to be found in the oldest democracies. For instance, 19th century British elections (after the expansion of the franchise to larger classes of people) were characterized by widespread voter pressure, vote-buying, 'treating,' and 'personation.'^['Treating' refers to the practice of plying voters with food and fortifying beverage before and after the vote; 'personation' refers to ineligible voters casting ballots on behalf of someone else.] Just like their modern descendants, those who sought to manipulate early democratic elections were embedded in hierarchical patronage networks. Laborers in the more agricultural counties often faced pressure from large landowners, via the tenant farmers who rented the land. In the boroughs, vote-buying was so common as to appear to many voters a normal part of the electoral process [@hoppenRoadsDemocracyElectioneering1996]; candidates relied on diverse agents to monitor local communities, distribute largess throughout the constituency, and mobilize voters [@campCatalystCauseLegislation2014]. 

Throughout the kingdom, candidates hired 'roughs' to blockade polling places, intimidate and harass opposing voters, interrupt opponents' meetings, and to defend themselves from the opposing side [@blaxillElectoralViolenceEngland2025]. Candidates relied on extensive networks to engage such workers, for two reasons. First, gentlemanly candidates might lack direct connections to the rougher sort of citizen. In the city of Norwich, candidates relied on publicans "who were well-known for their experience in this kind of business," to furnish roughs [@blaxillElectoralViolenceEngland2025]. Second, extended recruitment networks helped protect the candidates from liability for violence. As Blaxill et al [-@blaxillElectoralViolenceEngland2025] write, "roughs were hired by sub-agents, committee members or general prominent party supporters, thus providing a firebreak to the chief agent or candidate if the roughs themselves talked, freely or under detention" [@blaxillElectoralViolenceEngland2025, p. 191].

Such activities persisted unabated after the the passage of the Corrupt Practices Act of 1854 [@hoppenRoadsDemocracyElectioneering1996], which defined various electoral offenses but was largely toothless. Under the act, vote buyers---well-resourced politicians---faced the prospect of forfeiting 100 pounds, while vote sellers could forfeit ten. To initiate these proceedings against a lawbreaker anywhere in England, however, private citizens would have to sue in court in London [@ActConsolidateAmend]; this could entail a journey of several days. 

Only with the passage of the Illegal Practices Prevention Act of 1883 did these practices begin to diminish [@hoppenRoadsDemocracyElectioneering1996]. The 1883 Act put prosecution in the hands of the state, rather than individual citizens, allowed trials to be held in any relevant court, and increased the penalties for various electoral crimes [@IllegalPracticesPrevention]. Under the new law, those found guilty of bribery, treating, abduction of voters, undue influence, personation, or filing false campaign expenditure statements could face up to one year in prison (possibly to include hard labor), a 200-pound fine, the loss of voting rights, and the loss of the right to stand for election [@olearyEliminationCorruptPractices1962].

The Act also sought to break up politicians' patronage networks by limiting the number of electoral agents they could field and the maximum campaign expenses they could lawfully spend [@olearyEliminationCorruptPractices1962]. This, in combination with the fact that candidates could be held criminally liable for the misbehavior of their agents, helped lead to the decline of 'roughs' in British politics; increasingly large and professional police forces also helped [@blaxillElectoralViolenceEngland2025].  Parties and candidates went to great lengths to warn their agents to obey the law. "This Act is not to be trifled with," wrote one Conservative journal in 1896. "Its penalties amount to social ruin, and will, without doubt, be strictly enforced" [@rixEliminationCorruptPractices2008]. The effect of the law "was to transform the whole character of British electioneering within a generation" [@olearyEliminationCorruptPractices1962].

American elections in the 1800s also frequently featured 'treating,' ineligible or multiple voting, voter intimidation, ballot-stuffing, 'colonizing',^[Importing voters from a neighboring district.] 'cooping',^[The act of kidnapping and drugging individuals, and compelling them to vote (often more than once). See Bensel [-@benselAmericanBallotBox2004] for examples.] and outright fraud [@reynoldsSymbioticRelationshipVote1993;@benselAmericanBallotBox2004;@argersinger1985new;@cox1981turnout;@argersingerGreatConspiraciesStealing2024;@foleyBallotBattlesHistory2024;@summersPartyGamesGetting2004]---to say nothing of the systematic restrictions and repression aimed at Black citizens [@epperlyRuleViolenceRule2020]. These types of manipulation reached their apex in the United States' urban political machines, which sustained themselves through a mutually reinforcing cycle: election manipulation enabled the capture of political office, which allowed politicians to direct patronage resources (i.e. jobs, contracts), which in turn fueled further manipulation. 

Patronage---the funneling of jobs, contracts, and opportunities for graft to supporters---was essential to the operation of New York City's Tammany Hall machine, which dominated city politics for much of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. At its peak, the machine had the ability to distribute patronage on a massive scale, having allies in the governor, the mayor, the city comptroller, and more. Its most famous leader, William "Boss" Tweed, kept plum sources of jobs for himself as Commissioner of Public Works and executive roles in a variety of industries [@callowTweedRing1972]. "Control of patronage enabled Tweed to become New York's first absolute boss," Callow [-@callowTweedRing1972, p. 117] writes in his deep history of the Tammany machine. "From the ward leader down to the precinct captain, power depended on the ability to supply patronage to the faithful. ...through patronage alone [the machine] employed at least 12,000 people [and] 33 per cent of the money supplied to the city departments was stolen, in the sense that it went to men listed on the payrolls who did no work, or to payroll names which were fictitious." These men, in turn, were expected to deliver votes for the Tammany machine at election time.

American political machines were early pioneers in the use of what observers of post-Soviet politics would call "administrative resources" to control clients and influence elections [@Allina-Pisano2010]. Large corporations were extorted with the threat of tougher regulatory legislation. But small businesses---the merchant, innkeeper, stable owner, etc.---were extorted through the selective 'enforcement' of city ordinances. "...the bible of graft was the bulky volume of over 900 pages of city ordinances. The Ring used it to harass, blackmail, and demand illegitimate fees" [@callowTweedRing1972, p. 190]. Small businessmen who failed to pay the machine's fees or to turn out votes on election day faced the prospect of fines, closure, water shut-off, and other obstacles [@callowTweedRing1972, pp. 190-197].^[In this approach, the Tweed machine anticipated the tactics of bureaucratic extortion in the post-Soviet space [@vasilevaTrappedInformalityBig2018;@madlovicsPostcommunistPredationModeling2021].] 

Yet the success of Tammany Hall depended just as much on managing legal risks to its network of agents as it did on patronage resources. Indeed, control of patronage and control of the legal system each depended on the other, with election manipulation as the link. The Tammany machine owed its dominant position to the ability of its clients to deliver votes on election day. While many of these votes were honest---or at least not directly purchased or coerced---manipulation was an essential ingredient. Gangs of toughs were dispatched to drive away reformist voters, intimidate election judges, attack opposition toughs^[Reflecting later on this bygone era of politics, one politician lamented: "Nobody gets killed any
more and the ambulances and patrol wagons stay in their garages.... It was wonderful to see my men slug the opposition to preserve the sanctity of the ballot..." [@callowTweedRing1972, p. 209].], and to exercise their own franchise as often as they could. Pliant judges naturalized immigrants en masse, creating new voters sometimes at the pace of thousands a day. Voter registration lists were padded with the names of deceased and fictitious individuals. Tammany allies serving as election judges adjusted the results as needed. Votes were bought in cash, food, or liquor [@callowTweedRing1972, pp. 207 - 213]. 

All of these activities required that Tammany Hall be able to protect its agents from legal consequences. One of the machine's first orders of business was to secure the loyalty of the police, to install friendly judges in office, and to ensure that machine allies served as District Attorney. Friendly police officers, lawyers, and judges could help the alleged offender at any stage of the judicial process. One Tammany-affiliated prosecutor (who would later become mayor) was said to have prosecuted over 12,000 cases, but to have quashed 10,000 more [@callowTweedRing1972, p. 39]. The *Times* complained of this practice, writing that rather than bring indictments, the District Attorney "waits year after year for the benign influences of our Christian civilization to soften [suspects'] hearts. They naturally feel grateful for this forbearance...and testify their gratitude by working for him at elections" [@callowTweedRing1972, p. 148]. Well-connected lawyers worked hard on election day, getting those repeaters who were caught out of custody and back to work [@callowTweedRing1972, p. 150]. 

Despite these formidable resources, it could still be wise for front-line agents to take precautions to avoid detection. Disguises and costume changes were common. One Tammany Hall tough would rotate his gang of bearded repeaters through barbershops in between casting ballots [@callowTweedRing1972, p. 210]:

> When you've voted 'em with their whiskers on, you take 'em to a barber and scrape off the chin fringe. Then you vote 'em again with the side lilacs and a mustache. Then to a barber again, off comes the sides and you vote 'em a third time with the mustache. If that ain't enough and the box can stand a few more
ballots, clean off the mustache and vote 'em plain face.


As Callow writes [-@callowTweedRing1972, pp. 150-151]:

> The Tweed Ring, then, in consolidating its power, seized the legal machinery of New York to make it the backbone of its organization. Without it other operations like election fraud were in danger of exposure and prosecution. Thus the Ring helped to establish one of the classic patterns of a corrupt political machine. Its alliance with venal judges, the underworld, the police, and shyster lawyers kept the machine moving, providing not only patronage, jobs, and graft, but also the means to protect and control organized
crime. Fundamentally, however, it provided security and safety the legal obstructions to obscure public plunder. 

Though the political machines had formidable resources to deploy at election time, there were nevertheless large constituencies dissatisfied with their rule---these might include supporters of the local opposition party, those who resented the inefficiency and corruption of machine government, and professionals and corporations who desired a more regular legal environment [@summersPartyGamesGetting2004, p. 230]. At times of significant discontent, these constituencies could bring reformers to power. Reformers sought to break the power of the machine along both fronts that sustained it: by limiting politicians' freedom to distribute jobs (and the attendant opportunities for graft) to their clients, and by increasing the costliness of rigging elections. 
Civil service reform was the primary tool for constraining patronage and its influence on elections. Writing in 1919, a prominent reformer and Indiana politician argued that, just as the introduction of the Australian ballot removed the temptation to buy or coerce votes (by concealing whether the voter had in fact complied), the Pendleton Act of 1883 removed the incentive to "that kind of corruption which is nourished by the hope of office" [@foulkeFightingSpoilsmenReminiscences1919, p. 10]. 

The Pendleton Act granted protections from dismissal to certain classes of federal employees, established the Civil Service Commission, and mandated merit-based examinations for appointments to civil service jobs. In so doing it, limited the ability of incoming administrations to remove incumbents and open up jobs to their clients; it also limited their ability to reward influential clients with lucrative federal employment. While this directly cut down on federal patronage opportunities, it also indirectly cut into political machine's campaign war chests."At the heart of party finance," Summers writes, "was the principle of assessment on officeholders.... In return for being rewarded an office, the loyal partisan was expected to pay some of his or her salary to campaign funds" [-@summersPartyGamesGetting2004, p. 150]. The more lucrative the office, the larger the expected donation by the officeholder; those who failed to repay their patron's generosity could be dismissed in favor of someone more loyal.

The federal patronage system was the center of gravity for affiliated local machines; senators, representatives, and local bosses all had claims on the president's appointments within their domains [@foulkeFightingSpoilsmenReminiscences1919].  Federal civil service reform removed some of the choicest patronage prizes from the game, reducing the incentive to rig elections. Reformers pushed for similar changes at the municipal level, which naturally faced stiff resistance from the machines [@summersPartyGamesGetting2004].  



<!--The United States' political machines were undone by a combination of forces [@digaetanoWhyDidPolitical1985], including the rise of the programmatic welfare state, divisions within their own ranks, changing patterns of immigration and ethnicity, and successful efforts to limit the scope of political patronage. -->


Control over police departments and prosecutor's offices was an especially important battleground. Patronage-based police forces not only protected the machine's agents on election day, but also paid into the machine's coffers a share of the bribes and payoffs the department collected [@summersPartyGamesGetting2004, p. 155]. In one example of contestation over the police, the rivals of the Tammany machine, state-level Republicans, capitalized on public discontent to launch a state Senate investigation of the New York City police in 1893. The Lexow Committee report, containing over 1,000 pages of testimony of police interference with elections, concluded that "almost every conceivable crime against the elective franchise was either committed or permitted by the police," in the interests of Tammany Hall [@bermanTamingTigerLexow1980]. 

The committee's recommendations for police reform include a bipartisan supervisory board, and the creation of a civil service merit system for hiring and promotion of officers; these changes were incorporated into the reformed Greater New York charter of 1898 [@newyorkcityCharterGreaterNew1897], weakening partisan control over the police. While reformers and traditionalists would trade power over the years in New York and elsewhere [@bermanTamingTigerLexow1980;@walkerPopularJusticeHistory1980], these changes helped foster norms of professionalism and impartiality that would become enshrined in US Supreme Court doctrine, the manuals of the Department of Justice, and the guidelines of the American Bar Association [@greenWHENPROSECUTORSPOLITICK2020]. The norm of professional prosecution, "without fear or favor," helped uproot a long American tradition of election manipulation during the 20th century.

The mutually reinforcing loss of patronage resources and diminution of legal impunity intensified principal-agent problems within the machines. Even when machines were working properly, principal-agent problems abounded. Agents tasked with delivering votes could steal from the machine at a prodigious pace. One Pittsburgh boss dispatched two agents with $40,000 for 'election-day expenses' to an allied machine in Indianapolis; the men arrived, but the cash never did [@summersPartyGamesGetting2004, p. 11]. Disputes over finite patronage opportunities could fracture the machines. "The Ring and the Boss," wrote one observer of the machine era, "command an army composed of elements as dangerous as those which make up the crew of a pirate ship. The instant the slightest sign of weakness is shown, each man aspires to be commander, and is willing to sink the ship and all on board rather than to forego his own ambitious schemes" [@shapleySolidMulhoolyPolitical1889]. Indeed, the beginning of the end of Tweed era of Tammany Hall came when a highly-placed client, disgruntled over unpaid claims by the machine, leaked a trove of incriminating accounts to the *New York Times* [@callowTweedRing1972, pp. 259-260]. The Pendleton Act itself was passed, in part, due to the assassination of President Garfield by a disappointed office-seeker. 

To summarize, election manipulation in the early days of mass suffrage in the United Kingdom and United States bears a strong resemblance to the techniques we see in modern electoral authoritarian and electoral democratic regimes. Economic intimidation, vote-buying, violence, and falsification abounded, producing locally dominant political party machines. These efforts were organized along the lines of patronage networks, stretching from politicians and wealthy elites at the top down to the ordinary voter at the bottom. Rigged elections flourished when control over patronage also enabled legal impunity for election-manipulating agents. Reformers targeted both aspects of the machine in order to hold cleaner elections and capture power: the restrictions of patronage resources and the reduction of political control over police, prosecutors, and courts. 

## Part 3: Why do regime opponents protest?

Let us recapitulate the argument so far. Authoritarian incumbents manipulate elections in part to send signals of strength, and must recruit thousands of front-line agents to do so. These agents are motivated by the incumbent's patronage resources and by the desire to avoid individual punishment for lawbreaking. Incumbents are therefore constrained in their ability to manipulate by (possibly) three factors: the organizational cost of manipulation, agents' willingness to comply with their tasks, and the concern that manipulation will reduce the regime's legitimacy among the population. 

Legitimacy cost has frequently been conceptualized and measured as the likelihood of post-election protest. As a result, we cannot predict the level of manipulation desired by incumbents until we have a theoretical model of post-election protest. Put succinctly, if large-scale protests become much more likely as manipulation increases, then incumbents will have face high 'legitimacy costs' and have good reasons to minimize manipulation. If, instead, the likelihood of protest is *insensitive* to the level of manipulation, then incumbents will face lower legitimacy costs and less reason to restrain manipulation. Finally---to preview Chapter 3---if more extensive electoral manipulation actually makes it easier for incumbents to defeat protest movements, then manipulation could in fact *reduce* the 'legitimacy cost' of manipulation, creating a positive incentive for incumbents to manipulate more. While the first view, that protest risk can deter manipulation, is common in the literature, I argue that the latter two propositions are more theoretically grounded and empirically supported.

Why do potential protesters take to the streets or stay home? Theories which conclude that protest risk can deter manipulation typically assume that opposition protest is *elite-led and instrumental*. The opposition is typically modeled as a unitary, strategic actor who stages protest when the expected benefits of successfully overthrowing the incumbent outweighs the expected cost of failure. In these models, incumbents' use of manipulation reveals their low true popularity, and thus makes them appear more likely to lose a challenge in the streets [@Luo2017;@Little2012;@Schedler2002;@Beaulieu2014a]. Incumbents in these models therefore face a tradeoff between the short-term benefits of electoral manipulation (making winning the election more likely), and the risk that fraud will lead to protest [@Rozenas2016b]. As Beaulieu [-@Beaulieu2014a, p. 48] writes in this tradition, "As the opposition grows stronger, the amount of [manipulation] he will tolerate shrinks, and the incumbent who wishes to avoid protest will need to reduce the amount of manipulation she commits." 

This narrow view of protest is at odds with a broader understanding of political protest in authoritarian regimes, however. Electoral protest may occur because manipulation galvanizes citizens who hold diverse grievances [@tucker2007], because economic conditions are poor [@Brancati2016;@Beaulieu2014a], because electoral manipulation makes people angry [@Szakonyi2021], or simply because their party lost the election [@andersonLearningLoseElection2006]. Opposition elites, in turn, might seek to initiate---or amplify---protest to take advantage of this popular discontent for broad, rather than instrumental, reasons. They may wish to pressure the incumbent in order to push for improved competitiveness in the *next* election or to bargain for policy concessions [@chernykh2014;@robertson_protest_2010]. They may stage protests in order to identify new participants, forge new social ties [@barberaModelProtestsRevolution2019] and test new tactics. They may seek to communicate information about the government's unpopularity, to set the stage for larger, future protests [@lohmannDynamicsInformationalCascades1994]. Protests may be staged as part of internal factional rivalries within the opposition [@Buckles2017], or to drive media coverage of issues important to the opposition [@huangMediaProtestDiffusion2019;@jenningsStreetDemonstrationsMedia2019]. Indeed, opposition elites may take advantage of the bare fact of an election to challenge the incumbent, irrespective of the level of manipulation or the incumbent's vote-share [@Pop-Eleches2015].

In other words, there are many potential post-election protesters with various motivations. Some of these motivations are related to the level of manipulation, some cite the level of manipulation pretextually, and some are unrelated to election integrity at all. In line with this larger body of research, I argue that electoral protest in authoritarian regimes is best understood as *dispersed* and consequently *multi-purpose*. This theoretical distinction is important. If protest is primarily instrumental, opposition actors will only launch protests they think have a good chance of unseating the incumbent. If protest is dispersed and multipurpose, protest movements may initiate for reasons orthogonal to perceived incumbent strength and severity of electoral manipulation. In such a setting, incumbents cannot count on quiet streets simply by manipulating at a low level, or even holding clean elections.

The varied motivations for protest may help account for the inconsistent relationship between election manipulation and protest initiation found in the literature. Several cross-national studies have found links between election manipulation and binary measures of protest [@Brancati2016;@Harvey2020;@Hyde2014]. A study of African elections from 1997 to 2009 shows that election fraud is associated with an increased number of post-election conflicts [@daxecker2012]. Similar results are found by Rød [-@Rod2019], using a different measure of manipulation.  Using an alternative measure of manipulation from the NELDA dataset, however, Hafner-Burton et al [-@Hafner-Burton2016] find that the association between election fraud and post-election protest falls short of conventional statistical significance. Studies of one archetypal example, the 2011 election and protest cycle in Russia, have found a positive relationship between fraud and protest by some measures [@Lankina2017], and no relationship by others [@ananyevDictatorsSignalStrength2022]. As noted earlier, Simpser finds a negative relationship between the severity of election manipulation and the likelihood of protest [@simpser2013] and a positive relationship between 'excessive manipulation' (i.e. extensive manipulation and a large incumbent vote-share) and regime tenure. 



## Part 4: A regime-strength model of electoral manipulation

With the notion that the likelihood of post-election protest is likely to be insensitive to the level of manipulation, we can now build out a theory of electoral manipulation grounded in the incentives of incumbents, their agents, and potential protesters. Because this theory will argue that successful electoral manipulation requires the solution of significant principal-agent problems---and doing so sends signals about regime durability to elites---I call this the *regime-strength model of electoral manipulation*. 

There are two major dimensions to this argument. First, I argue that the same capacities that incumbents rely on to manipulate elections---patronage resources and impunity for agents---are useful for defeating protest movements. Consequently, incumbent regimes that manipulate elections extensively are intrinsically likely to have the tools needed to survive post-election protests. This means that incumbents who are capable of extensive manipulation face reduced legitimacy costs from that same manipulation; they are more likely to survive the possible backlash. 

Second, expanding upon Simpser's work [-@simpser2013] I argue that extensive electoral manipulation sends signals about these resources and capacities to elites, which incentivize them to cooperate with the incumbent during protest movements. Because it requires the resolution of significant principal-agent problems, extensive electoral manipulation is a costly signal of the incumbent's patronage resources, control over the security environment and the courts, and ability to command agent loyalty broadly across the territory of the country. It further signals the regime's intention to devote resources within the elite selectorate, rather than more broadly among society. The more extensive the manipulation, the stronger these signals in favor of elite solidarity are likely to be. 

This model extends Simpser's work in two ways. First, it grounds the costly nature of the strength signal in the principal-agent dynamic; if manipulation could simply be willed into existence by the incumbent, it would not be not costly [@Harvey2020]. By overcoming a huge set of principal-agent problems, the incumbent 'pays' to display his patronage capacity and influence over agents. This is a fundamental reason why electoral manipulation is not cheap talk, as some deterrence models posit. Second, I argue that these signals do not require manipulation to be extensive or blatant, as in Simpser [-@simpser2013]. To be successful in this regard, manipulation need not result in a wide margin of victory or be carried out in plain view; it is only necessary that the manipulation effort be intelligible to elites themselves.

### Resources and capacities

As we have seen, incumbents who wish to produce extensive electoral manipulation must have deep patronage resources [@Harvey2019;@hale_patronal_2014;@greene_why_2007] and the ability to shield agents from the consequences of breaking the law. These resources and capacities improve the incumbent's ability to respond to a nascent protest movement through repression or concessions [@tillyMobilizationRevolution1978;@lipskyProtest1968;@Hummel2019;@raslerConcessionsRepression1996;@Bishara2015;@Frantz2014]. Concessions may be aimed at protesting parties themselves [@reuter2015;@mooreRepressionDissentSubstitution2000;@Hafner-Burton2016;@Piven1979] or the more moderate public, in order to keep them on the sidelines of the conflict [@Hummel2019]. Incumbents may also threaten to withhold resources from clients in exchange for passive support [@Rosenfeld2017], sapping the pool of potential protesters.   

Ruling parties may also lean on repression, calling upon the security services to disperse protests, arrest leaders, and perhaps employ harsher methods including disappearance, torture, and execution [@Escriba_Folch2013;@Davenport2007]. Though such crackdowns risk provoking a backlash, they are aimed at demobilizing the opposition by increasing the costs of participation in overt dissent [@DeVogel2022]. The ability to protect regime agents from any legal consequences for carrying out orders, a condition which helps enable illegal election manipulation [@Harvey2022], is also an asset when asking law enforcement agents to carry out possibly violent repression [@MAGALONI_RODRIGUEZ_2020;@stavro_police_2023;@abouharbFactoJudicialIndependence2013]. Additionally, more consolidated control over patronage resources can help incentivize elite unity [@Reuter2019;@hale_patronal_2014;@Arriola_2009], which can enable repression by the security forces [@hendrix_2017;@Frugé_2019;@Albrecht_Ohl_2016].

As a short-hand, I refer to this as "control-based" strength---those sources of regime durability that derive from its ability to mobilize and discipline agents, to distribute patronage, and to deploy coercion. This contrasts with the legitimacy-based view of strength centered in the regime-weakness framework. This argument---that successful, large-scale election manipulation draws on some of the same resources a state may use to suppress protest---turns the deterrent logic on its head. Instead of signalling weakness, large-scale fraud indicates a well of resilience: control over resources, impunity for pro-regime lawbreaking, and loyal agents. As a result, governments that build and deploy an electoral manipulation apparatus may simultaneously be inoculating themselves against the expected cost of protest. 

### Costly signals and elite solidarity



Protest movements not not only threaten the incumbent directly; they can also create the conditions for elite splits and coups d'etat. Elites in authoritarian regimes have resources they control. When incumbents offer elites a favorable distribution of resources, elites can use their resources to support the incumbent; if a challenger offers a better deal, they can rebel [@BuenodeMesquita2005;@svolik_politics_2012]. The emergence of electoral protest can expand splits in the elite, among hardliners who prefer the continuation or intensification of authoritarianism, and softliners who are willing to tolerate reforms [@odonnellTransitionsAuthoritarianRule2013;@Schedler2002]. Large-scale, nonviolent protest can induce defections among the incumbent's elite supporters, contributing to protest success [@Chenoweth_Stephan2011]. Extensive electoral manipulation acts as a costly signal of a) the incumbent's capacities (resources and agent impunity) b) his intention to continue a favorable distribution of resources to elites, and c) if enshrined in the electoral outcome, provides a commitment mechanism for that distribution.

Main ideas to get across here: 

- Electoral manipulation is a costly investment in reducing mass input in political decisions for the next term (selectorate theory in authoritarian regimes---cleaner elections increase the size of the selectorate / WC, meaning more public goods and less private goods. Manipulation prevents this. 
- This commitment is credible: The expenditure, first, is kept 'in house' by channeling resources through the manipulation network rather than through popular campaign promises. Limited campaign promises  + costly effort to rig votes means commitment to elites more credible.
- The election, if upheld, locks in that favorable bargain for the next term (4+ years). If election overturned, uncertainty and possible democratization--bad for elites.  
- This works even when manipulation is not excessive; actually, especially when elections are close and manipulation is high.
  - In this case, elites know they have the most to lose from re-drawing the bargain. If manipulation is high and margin of victory low, that means status quo is very unpopular. Cleaner election re-do will lead to bigger upset of the distribution of resources in favor of citizens. The more extensive the manipulation the more the current selectorate has to lose if the election is annulled or the government overthrown.
- Blatant is also not necessary, as long as elites are plugged into the level of covert manipulation. This is plausible, but will need cites. Rundlett and svolik might help here.

In addition, as Gehlbach and Simpser [-@gehlbach2015electoral] argue, effective electoral manipulation can induce regime agents to exert effort on behalf of the incumbent. Elite defections, which can presage real challenges for the incumbent during a crisis, are also rarer in less democratic regions, where election manipulation is likely more severe [@Reuter2019]. Just as election manipulation has been held to solve a coordination problem for regime opponents, it may also solve a coordination problem for regime agents: when successful, a campaign to manufacture votes signals to agents that other agents are likely to stick with the incumbent due to its revealed capacities [@hale_patronal_2014]. 




Cut text:

These divergent incentives can create a classic principal-agent problem. Because principals cannot perfectly monitor their agents' behavior, an agent may attempt to shirk her assigned manipulation tasks while still hoping to retain her place in the patronage network---pocketing the reward without bearing the risk.

In order to solve these problems, and ensure that a directive to manipulate the election issued at the top of the pyramid is in fact carried out across the bottom, incumbents need three things. First, incumbents must have access to benefits that can be shared with subordinates, to reward them for their efforts. Front-line agents do not directly benefit from each manufactured vote they generate. Instead, agents perform their assigned tasks in order to remain embedded within a principal’s patronage network.



Finally, the incumbent must be able to convince his subordinates that he will remain in power through the election and beyond; that is, that his ability to mete out rewards and punishments will be lasting [@hale_patronal_2014;@gehlbach2015electoral;@simpser2013]. If the principal appears less likely to control access to patronage due to electoral defeat or intraparty rivalry, her offer of post-election patronage will appear less viable to agents, reducing their incentive to work on her behalf [@hale_democracy_2006]. When one patronage network controls a large share of resources, agents have a strong incentive to support the principal: access to rents and resources outside that network is limited, competing offers of patronage by opposition figures are necessarily discounted, and punishment of defectors by exclusion from the network seems assured [@hale_patronal_2014]. In a society characterized by multiple patronage networks, by contrast, the credibility of an individual principal’s offer is contingent on the likelihood that the principal will win the election or leadership struggle. As a result, clients ‘hedge their bets or pin their hopes on different networks in an uncoordinated fashion’ [@hale_patronal_2014, p. 72]. Consequently, agents are more strongly incentivized to participate in electoral manipulation efforts when patronage networks are more consolidated. 

Finally, manipulation on a national scale can be very expensive, and principals’ resources are not limitless. Even relatively cost-effective tactics like co-opting employers to pressure voters requires monitoring efforts and rewards for compliant businesses [@frye2014, p. 207]. Agents and brokers engaged in falsification or other types of manipulation must still be organized and compensated [@Langston2009mexico]. Vote-buying, however, is especially costly [@lehoucq2002;@wang2007], and such efforts become increasingly expensive as competitiveness increases [@corstange2018clientelism]. As a result, incumbents are likely to prefer centralized forms of manipulation in low risk areas, due to their cost-effectiveness. This pattern has been documented both domestically in Russia [@harvey_manipulation_2016] and cross-nationally [@vanham2015sticks]. Consequently, if higher local constraints make agents less willing to tamper with elections in administrative ways, principals may find agents both more expensive to hire (as they turn toward vote-buying and similar tactics) and more likely to shirk their duties on election day (as they become harder to monitor). This limits the ability of principals to compensate for higher competitiveness by boosting payments for agents.
